approach_name: Chronological spine with spiral returns: world history from level 1 to university
approach_summary: One timeline from the first humans to today, told three times at rising depth. Levels 1-3 start from the child's world then and now and from the deep past. Levels 4-6 run from human origins to about 500 CE, and level 6 gives a first look at every age, including Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Middle East. Levels 7-9 run from about 300 to 1900. Level 10 covers 1848-1945 on Cambridge IGCSE. Level 11 covers the world since 1945, with IGCSE Option B for the Cold War and the other layers for decolonisation, rights, globalisation and the environment. Level 12 adds AS Level depth and comparison across eras, and U deals with evidence, myths and debate. A timeline gives every card one clear place in time. Each age returns in every tier, so pupils in Tanzania and Bhutan meet their own history early, and rows by region at 12 and U give depth. Strands for everyday life, belief, trade, science, rights, environment and power cut across the eras, with ideas and development before wars and kings.

standard_choice.primary: Three layers. Content spine: World History for Us All, Big Eras 1-9. Outcome wording: NCHS National Standards for History, Basic Edition 1996. Named exam standard for levels 10 to U: Cambridge IGCSE History 0470, same content as IGCSE 0977 and O Level 2147, and Cambridge International AS & A Level History 9489. University benchmark: AP World History: Modern, from about 1200.
supporting: Cambridge Primary Humanities 0065 and Lower Secondary Humanities 0839, Past strand, for skill wording at levels 1-9, such as objective 789PTsk.04
Big History Project thresholds and units, as an opening frame only
Tanzania 2023 syllabi from the Tanzania Institute of Education: Historia ya Tanzania na Maadili, HTM, for Standard III-VI and Form I-IV, and History for Form I-IV and Form V-VI
Bhutan History Curriculum Framework 2022, Classes VII-XII, and Social Studies Instructional Guide IV-VI, 2025

IB PYP Social studies scope and sequence 2008, which may since have been superseded, IB MYP Individuals and societies, and IB DP History, current guide and new guide for first assessment 2028, cited as references only, never as endorsement
standard_choice.rationale: No international test covers history: TIMSS tests mathematics and science, and PISA reading, mathematics and science. So we map to frameworks in three layers. The spine is World History for Us All from UCLA, whose nine Big Eras run from the first humans in Africa to today as one connected story. Outcome wording comes from the US National Standards for History, 1996, the only framework we found that runs from kindergarten to grade 12 with a grade band, such as K-4 or 9-12, on each outcome. We place each outcome in one year of its band and use only the world-history parts. For levels 10 to U we name Cambridge IGCSE History 0470, the same content as O Level 2147, and AS & A Level History 9489. IGCSE is taught in over 150 countries, and Cambridge says O Level is designed for learners whose first language may not be English. Bhutan has been aligning its curriculum with Cambridge standards since January 2025, but has not said whether History is included. Cambridge key questions name people, places and treaties, so they turn straight into four-option cards, but Cambridge has no history content below level 10 and examines nothing before 1774. For university we add AP World History: Modern, which the College Board says is designed to be the equivalent of an introductory college survey of modern world history. It uses four-option questions and starts about 1200, so earlier periods use the grade 9-12 National Standards. All eleven topics that India, Kenya, Brazil and England share have rows; Tanzania and Bhutan guided relevance. The set covers every IGCSE core key question, all five depth studies and most AS and A Level topics, far beyond one candidate's options. Cards fit Cambridge AO1 and AO2 well, and AO3 and AO4 only in part.
standard_choice.not_used: ICCS tests civic knowledge in grade 8 and is background only. The IB is not primary: PYP and MYP prescribe no content, DP content starts in 750 CE and is option-based, and IB guidance limits the commercial use of IB materials and of the IB name, so we cite IB documents only as references and claim no IB alignment or endorsement. Cambridge alone cannot be the spine, since about 60 of the 80 existing sets have no Cambridge anchor. Big History is mostly cosmology and biology. National curricula are not international standards: Tanzania's HTM is taught in Kiswahili and is value-led, and Bhutan gives 50-70 percent of history time to Bhutan History and Civics, so they guide relevance, not outcome wording.

tiers.focus: Level 1 is the child's world then and now, with time, family, homes, travel, festivals and leaders. Level 2 covers human ancestors in East Africa, Stone Age life, and family life then and now in two places. Level 3 covers first farmers, towns and cities, writing, money, famous places, journeys and helpers from every continent. All new.
tiers.card_style: Level 1 about 15 to 25 words in 3 to 6 sentences, no glossary, one-word options, written to be read aloud by a teacher or parent. Level 2 about 40 words in 3 to 6 sentences, at most one glossary word. Level 3 about 60 to 70 words in 5 to 9 sentences on the front, as on the sample card about paper, with up to three glossary words on the back. The picture shows the setting or one clue, never the answer, and no question asks what the picture shows. One concrete thing per card. Questions: which one, what was it for, which came first, then or now. Nothing frightening.

tiers.focus: Levels 4-5: human origins to about 500 CE, Big Eras 1-4, with farming, river civilisations, early states in Africa, Asia and the Americas, traditional leadership, early belief and classical empires. Level 6: the 80 existing level-6 cards plus first-look cards on Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Middle East, so every pupil meets the whole timeline once.
tiers.card_style: House format, about 80 to 110 words in 7 to 12 sentences of about seven words, glossary for words outside the 1,000 most common. Anonymised clue chain. Questions: identify, order two events, one simple cause or result. Centuries, not exact years. Belief marked as belief.

tiers.focus: About 300 to 1900, Big Eras 5-7. Level 7: Islam and the medieval worlds of Africa, Asia, Europe, the Americas and the Pacific, and how we know about states with few written records. Level 8: 1450-1800, with voyages, the Columbian Exchange, slave trades, land empires, and limited and absolute monarchy. Level 9: 1750-1900, with revolutions, industry, abolition, migration and conquest, plus the 80 existing level-9 cards.
tiers.card_style: About 100 to 130 words in 9 to 12 sentences, three to five glossary words, two or three linked clues across regions or from cause to effect. Questions on cause and consequence, comparison, change over time and how we know. Key dates allowed. Conquest and slavery told from more than one side, no gore.

tiers.focus: Level 10: 1848-1945 on Cambridge IGCSE Option A, Option B key questions 1-3 and depth studies A-E. Level 11: the world since 1945, with IGCSE Option B key questions 4-6 for the Cold War and the other layers for decolonisation, rights, globalisation and the environment. Level 12: Cambridge AS Level depth and comparison across eras, with 160 existing cards. U: A Level Papers 3 and 4, AP World History: Modern and the NCHS grade 9-12 standards, for evidence, myths and interpretations, with 80 existing cards.
tiers.card_style: About 110 to 140 words in 9 to 12 short sentences, with abstract terms such as mandate or interpretation in the glossary. Levels 10-11 ask for causes, results and significance; 12 compares and tracks change; U asks which evidence supports a claim or which view a historian holds. One defensible answer of four. Sensitive topics through facts and testimony, with no victim images.

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 9, students can explain why millions moved to new lands in the 1800s, such as Indian workers to East Africa, and give one push and one pull reason.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: WHFUA Big Era 7, Landscape 7.4; NCERT Class 10, indentured labour

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 10, students can explain why revolutions broke out across Europe in 1848 and how Italy and Germany became united nation states.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge IGCSE 0470 Option A, key questions 1-3; Cambridge 9489 AS European option, Germany 1815-71

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 10, students can explain why the United States fought a civil war and what the war and Reconstruction changed for enslaved people.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge IGCSE 0470 Option A, key question 4; Cambridge 9489 AS American option, Civil War and Reconstruction

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 10, students can compare direct, indirect and private colonial rule, using Senegal, Nigeria and the Congo Free State.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge IGCSE 0470 Option A, key question 5; Cambridge 9489 AS key question 7.1; Kenya KICD Senior School Grade 11

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 10, students can explain the main causes of the First World War and how it was also fought in Africa, the Middle East and Asia.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge IGCSE 0470 Option A, key question 6, and depth study A, key question 2; NCHS World History Era 8, Standard 2

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 10, students can describe the peace of 1919 and the League of Nations, and why the League failed in Manchuria and Abyssinia.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge IGCSE 0470 Option B, key questions 1 and 2; Tanzania History A-level 2023, Form VI

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 10, students can explain how dictators took power in Russia, Italy and Germany, and how the crash of 1929 helped extreme parties win support.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge IGCSE 0470 depth studies B, C and D; Cambridge 9489 Paper 4 European option

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 10, students can describe how peoples in Asia, Africa and Latin America pushed for land, rights and self-rule from 1900 to 1945, such as in Mexico, China, India and Nigeria.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: WHFUA Big Era 8, Landscape 8.4; NCHS World History Era 8, 1B and 3B; Tanzania History O-level 2023, Form III

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 10, students can describe turning points of the Second World War in Europe, Africa and Asia, and the Holocaust as the planned murder of about six million Jews, alongside the Nazi murder of Roma, disabled people and others.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge IGCSE 0470 depth study E, and depth study B for the Holocaust; Cambridge 9489 Paper 3, The Holocaust; NCHS World History Era 8, 4B; Kenya KICD Senior School Grade 10, global wars and Africa; England National Curriculum 2013, KS3, Holocaust statutory

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 11, students can explain why the USA and the Soviet Union became rivals, describe crises such as Berlin, Korea, Cuba and Vietnam, and say how the Cold War ended.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge IGCSE 0470 Option B, key questions 4-6; WHFUA Big Era 9, Landscape 9.2

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 11, students can describe how countries in Asia, Africa and the Middle East won independence after 1945, and name leaders such as Nehru, Sukarno, Nkrumah and Nyerere.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: NCHS World History Era 9, 1C; Cambridge 9489 Paper 4, key question 9.4; BNCC EF09HI31

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 11, students can describe the path a country chose after 1945, such as non-alignment in India, ujamaa in Tanzania or Gross National Happiness in Bhutan, and one problem it met.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: NCHS World History Era 9, 1C; Kenya KICD Senior School Grade 11, Non-Aligned Movement; Tanzania HTM primary 2023, Std VI; Bhutan History Framework 2022, Class X

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 11, students can describe the work of the United Nations and movements for equal rights, such as civil rights in the USA, the fight against apartheid and women's movements.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: NCHS World History Era 9, 1A and Standard 2; Cambridge 9489 Paper 4, key questions 5.3 and 8.3; Tanzania History O-level 2023, Form IV

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 11, students can describe how vaccines, new seeds, space flight, computers and mobile money changed life after 1945, with one benefit and one problem.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: NCHS World History Era 9, 2E; WHFUA Big Era 9, Landscape 9.5

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 11, students can describe how the world economy became more connected, such as container ships, China's reforms after 1978 and falling extreme poverty.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: WHFUA Big Era 9, Landscapes 9.1 and 9.4; AP World History: Modern Unit 9; Tanzania HTM Form IV 2023

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 11, students can describe how human activity changed the climate and environment, and name shared efforts such as the Montreal Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: WHFUA Big Era 9, Landscape 9.6; AP World History: Modern theme Humans and the Environment

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 11, students can describe conflicts after 1945 outside the Cold War, such as in the Middle East, Rwanda and former Yugoslavia, and efforts to end them.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: NCHS World History Era 9, Standard 2; Tanzania History A-level 2023, Form VI, Camp David, Oslo, Kosovo, Rwanda; BNCC 9th year, Palestine

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 12, students can tell long-term causes from short-term triggers, and short-lived results from lasting ones, for key events from every era, such as the fall of Rome or the end of apartheid.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 AO2, cause and consequence; NCHS Historical Thinking Standard 3; NCHS World History Across the Eras

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 12, students can compare how societies dealt with the same problem, such as ruling a large empire or living with many faiths.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 key concept similarity and difference; AP World History: Modern reasoning process Comparison; NCHS World History Era 4, 2B

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 12, students can identify what changed and what stayed the same over long periods, such as trade routes, religions, work or women's rights.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 key concept change and continuity; AP World History: Modern reasoning process Continuity and Change

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 12, students can explain the significance of a person or event: why it mattered then and why it is still remembered.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 key concept significance; Cambridge IGCSE 0470 Component 3, significance

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 12, students can explain how the French Revolution moved from reform in 1789 to the Terror and then to Napoleon, and why the Russian tsar fell in 1917.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 AS European option, key question 1.1, France 1774-1814 and Russia 1881-1924

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 12, students can compare why some responses to imperialism after 1870 succeeded and others failed, such as Ethiopia at Adwa, Meiji Japan, the Zulu kingdom and the Maji Maji war.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 AS International option, key questions 7.1 and 7.3; Tanzania HTM Form II 2023, resistance to colonial invasion

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 12, students can name the type of source behind a past event and one limit of it, such as a king's inscription or a chronicle by the winners.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 AO3; NCHS Historical Thinking Standards 2 and 4, identify the source and test its credibility; Bhutan History Framework 2022, Class XI

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of level 12, students can explain how ideas of rights grew from the declarations of the 1770s and 1780s, through campaigns against slavery and empire, to the Universal Declaration of 1948, which drafters from India, China, Lebanon and Latin America helped shape, and who was left out.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 AS key question 1.1; NCHS World History Era 9, Standard 2; Kenya KICD Senior School Grade 11

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of university level, students can recognise that historians interpret events differently, and name a debate, such as blame for the First World War or whether Rome fell or slowly changed.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 AO4 and Paper 3; AP World History: Modern Skill 3, Claims and Evidence in Sources; NCHS Historical Thinking Standard 3, debates among historians; IB DP AO3, reference only

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of university level, students can say how reliable a type of evidence is, such as an inscription, a traveller's account, an oral tradition or a later legend, and why.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 AO3; AP World History: Modern Skill 2, Sourcing and Situation; NCHS Historical Thinking Standard 4

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of university level, students can identify myths about famous people and events and say what the evidence shows instead.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: NCHS Historical Thinking Standard 3; AP World History: Modern Skill 3, Claims and Evidence in Sources

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of university level, students can explain long-term patterns, such as the spread of farming, growing exchange networks, why industry began in Britain and the great acceleration after 1945.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: NCHS World History Across the Eras; WHFUA Big Era 8, Landscape 8.7, and Big Era 9, Landscape 9.6; AP World History: Modern Units 2, 4, 5 and 9

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of university level, students can explain how historians' questions widened to include ordinary people, women, colonised peoples and the environment.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 AO4; Bhutan History Framework 2022, Class XII, schools of historiography

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of university level, students can explain how records, testimony and places show what happened in the Holocaust and in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda, and why denial goes against the evidence.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: Cambridge 9489 Paper 3, The Holocaust; NCHS World History Era 8, 4B; Tanzania History A-level 2023, Form VI

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of university level, students can explain why a discovery is usually the work of many people and earlier ideas from several regions, not of one genius.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: NCHS Historical Thinking Standard 3, multiple causation and the importance of the individual; WHFUA key theme Science, Technology, and the Environment

level_outcomes.statement: By the end of university level, students can explain when, by whom and why the sources about a religious founder were written, and what historians can and cannot know from them.
level_outcomes.standard_refs: AP World History: Modern Skill 2, Sourcing and Situation; Cambridge 9489 AO3; Tanzania History A-level 2023, Form V

totals_note: 1,519 cards: 400 existing and 1,119 new. Tier 1-3: 223 new; level 1 51, level 2 68, level 3 104. Tier 4-6: 80 existing plus 240 new, 320 in all; level 4 62, level 5 87, level 6 171, of which 80 existing. Tier 7-9: 80 plus 325, 405; level 7 120, level 8 100, level 9 185, of which 80 existing. Tier 10-U: 240 plus 331, 571; level 10 89, level 11 125, level 12 238, of which 160 existing, U 119, of which 80 existing. Every row's notes begin with its cards by level, so these totals can be checked. Most levels get about 90 to 125 cards, two or three a week. Level 1 has fewer because each card holds one fact and is read aloud; level 4 has fewer because it covers only the first humans to the first metals; levels 6, 9 and 12 hold the existing sets. Era-tagged cards: Big Eras 1-2 5 percent, 3 9, 4 13, 5 18, 6 16, 7 15, 8 10, 9 14, close to the NCHS weights; 137 cards run across time. Region shares count each row by its main region and each existing card by its own set, and leave out Global rows, which hold 29 percent of all cards: Africa 24, Asia and Pacific 24, Latin America plus Middle East 19, Europe plus North America 33 percent; new cards alone 32, 29, 18 and 22. New cards by strand: power and government 22 percent, empire 6 and conflict 4, against 64 percent for everyday life, science, belief, trade, evidence and environment. Status planned means the topic is already on the Akelius topic list; all 54 unproduced topics on that list have a row, with their numbers in the notes. Phase 1 is 553 new cards in 83 rows: every planned topic, at least one row for every outcome, the pilot rows and the most local Tanzania and Bhutan rows. With the existing cards that makes 953, split Africa 38, Asia 21, Latin America plus Middle East 17 and Europe plus North America 24 percent. Phase 2 is the other 566. Order. Step 0: refill image credits, finish the 256 missing images of the existing sets and rebuild. Step 1: extend import_cards.py, apply_translations.py, build_prompts.py and build_index.py to 1-12 cards per file, levels 1-12 and U printed as H 1 to H U, and sentence ranges by level, 3 to 6 at levels 1-2, 5 to 9 at level 3 and 7 to 12 from level 4; add level 1-3 rules to the writing rules. Step 2: decisions from Roger and Jonas on levels 1-2, three-card sets and size. Step 3: a pilot of about 30 cards for Daniel and Roger: T1-3-016 with Daniel's paper card, one card each at levels 1 and 2, T7-9-044 with Daniel's monarchy example, and T10-U-035. Step 4: planned rows in list order: science and mathematics, T7-9-054, T10-U-023, T7-9-025, T4-6-025 and T4-6-030; Africa, T4-6-014, T4-6-033, T7-9-014, T7-9-034 and T10-U-049; Asia, T7-9-008, T7-9-019, T7-9-041 and T7-9-059; then the four five-card topics, T10-U-036, T10-U-039, T10-U-053 and T7-9-053. Step 5: Africa and Asia gap rows, one region and era per run, so overlapping motifs are reviewed together. Step 6: the tier 1-3 bulk after the pilot is approved. Step 7: the Cambridge rows for levels 10-11. Step 8: the remaining Europe and Global rows. Runs are serial: at 25-35 cards a run, phase 1 takes 16-22 runs and the whole map 32-45. Main changes after the review: 1. Fixed eleven history errors: human ancestors called the first humans, unchecked human-origin dates, Kush and Caral placed beyond the river valleys, the first towns placed by rivers, Cai Lun as inventor of paper and Han exams, the Talas paper legend, the Cyrus Cylinder, plague in China stated as fact, the Crusades as the route of learning, Chinese workers in East Africa, and 1948 named from one side only. 2. Added guards in the notes against further myths and slips: barter first, single origins for zero and geometry, one fire at Alexandria, Constantine and the state religion, an Ottoman printing ban, Ibn Majid as da Gama's pilot, Westphalia, Rapa Nui, an Aryan invasion, Quetzalcoatl, the Iroquois and the US constitution, Rosa Parks, Lovelace and Seacole, Bagamoyo, the Moon and the Great Wall, Dutch Indonesia, 1904-05, Achebe's era, dogs, Gobekli Tepe and the Zhabdrung. 3. More women, ordinary people and non-European voices: medieval women, enslaved people's own revolts and abolition in Zanzibar and Tanganyika, Asian and African thinkers and scientists, the Asian, Arab and Latin American drafters of the 1948 declaration, women resistance leaders, Bibi Titi Mohamed and the Aba Women's War, and the hard chapters of Tanzanian and Bhutanese history. 4. New rows: African and local religions, refugees since 1945, the USA from the Gilded Age to 1993, how we know at levels 7-9, climate shocks before 1900, and a separate Bhutan heritage row. 5. Outcomes: 103 in all, 7 at level 1 and 8 at every other level. New H2.7, H2.8 and H7.7. Rewritten so that levels build on each other, H4.1, H4.4, H4.5, H5.1, H12.1, H12.5 and H12.6; so that one card can test them, H3.5, H3.6, H4.8 and H5.2; and the two catch-alls H6.7 and H9.7. Daily life in Tanzania and Bhutan today is no longer called long ago. 6. Every row's levels now match its outcomes, including the existing grade-12 and university cards. Every row and outcome now leads with WHFUA, NCHS, Cambridge or AP, about 30 codes were corrected, and the internal topic-list references moved to the notes. 7. Repeats removed: new cards no longer re-teach facts, people or images the 400 existing cards use, names in existing card text are context and not new answers, and each fact has one owning row. Science rows rose to the planned counts and war rows fell, so new cards went from 1,128 to 1,119 despite the added rows. 8. The standard choice now names three layers, syllabus versions, the Bhutan and AP limits, the IB wording and a true coverage claim. 9. Notes now say why, regions come from a fixed list, eras carry dates, and each row has a phase. 10. Conflicts between reviews: the village row T1-3-030 is kept and renamed instead of merged into T1-3-003; mobile money stays as the now end of the level-3 money row, with its history in T10-U-053; Polynesian sailors stay at level 3 with a facet T7-9-020 does not use; appeasement in T10-U-021 and the Cold War's origins in T10-U-025 stay, so the IGCSE coverage claim holds; six classical rows got a level-5 outcome instead of moving wholly to level 6, which keeps level 5 near 90 cards; the merge of H10.4 and H10.5 was not made. card_numbers_note: About 1,500 cards in all: the 400 that exist and 1,119 new. Tier 1-3: 223 new cards. Tier 4-6: 320 cards, of which 80 exist. Tier 7-9: 405 cards, of which 80 exist. Tier 10-U: 571 cards, of which 240 exist. Most levels get about 90 to 125 cards, two or three a week over a school year. Level 1 has fewer, since each card holds one fact and is read aloud, and level 4 covers only the first humans to the first metals. The Cards by level sheet gives the number for every row and level. We suggest two phases. Phase 1 has 553 new cards, about 950 with the existing ones, and covers every outcome at least once, every topic already on our list and the topics closest to pupils in Tanzania and Bhutan. Phase 2 adds the remaining 566 cards for depth.
